title: Ignoring the effects of photovoltaic array deployment on greenhouse gas emissions may lead to overestimation of the contribution of photovoltaic power generation to greenhouse gas reduction
abstract: Photovoltaic (PV) power generation is one of the world’s most promising options for carbon emission reduction. However, whether the operation period of solar parks can increase greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in hosting natural ecosystems has not been fully considered. Here, we conducted a field experiment to compensate for the lack of evaluation of the effects of PV array deployment on GHG emissions. Our results show that the PV arrays caused significant differences in air microclimate, soil properties, and vegetation characteristics. Simultaneously, PV arrays had more significant effects on CO2 and N2O emissions but a minor impact on CH4 uptake in the growing season. Of all the environmental variables included, soil temperature and moisture were the main drivers of GHG flux variation. The sustained flux global warming potential from the PV arrays significantly increased by 8.14% compared to the ambient grassland. Our evaluation models identified that the GHG footprint of PV arrays during the operation period on grasslands was 20.62 g CO2-eq kW h–1. Compared with our model estimates, GHG footprint estimates reported in previous studies were generally less by 25.46–50.76%. The contribution of PV power generation to GHG reduction may be overestimated without considering the impact of PV arrays on hosting ecosystems.

## **the of Photovoltaic on Ignoring Effects Array Deployment Greenhouse Gas Emissions May Lead to Overestimation of the Contribution of Photovoltaic Power Generation to Greenhouse Gas Reduction**

Bin Zhang, Ruohui Zhang, You Li, Shiwen Wang, and Fu Xing*

**Cite This:** _Environ. Sci. Technol._ 2023, 57, 4241−4252 **Read Online**

ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations * **sı** Supporting Information

ABSTRACT: Photovoltaic (PV) power generation is one of the world’s most promising options for carbon emission reduction. However, whether the operation period of solar parks can increase greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in hosting natural ecosystems has not been fully considered. Here, we conducted a field experiment to compensate for the lack of evaluation of the effects of PV array deployment on GHG emissions. Our results show that the PV arrays caused significant differences in air microclimate, soil properties, and vegetation characteristics. Simultaneously, PV arrays had more significant effects on CO2 and N2O emissions but a minor impact on CH4 uptake in the growing season. Of all the environmental variables included, soil temperature and moisture were the main drivers of GHG flux variation. The sustained flux global warming potential from the PV arrays significantly increased by 8.14% compared to the ambient grassland. Our evaluation models identified that the

GHG footprint of PV arrays during the operation period on grasslands was 20.62 g CO2-eq kW h[−][1] . Compared with our model estimates, GHG footprint estimates reported in previous studies were generally less by 25.46−50.76%. The contribution of PV power generation to GHG reduction may be overestimated without considering the impact of PV arrays on hosting ecosystems. KEYWORDS: _renewable energy, solar parks, carbon footprint, microclimate, greenhouse gas_

## ■ **[INTRODUCTION]**

To cope with the serious situation of climate change, carbon emission reduction has become the common consensus worldwide.[1] Many countries have set a goal for carbon neutrality.[2] Solar photovoltaics (PV) has the greatest potential to achieve this goal; PV power accounts for about 20 to 60 percent of the global electricity scenario in a largely or fully decarbonized context by 2050.[3] Due to the lower power density of PV power compared to fossil energy, a large amount of land will be required to accommodate PV facilities in the future.[4] The management of solar parks as pasture is an ideal option in terms of reducing emissions from land use change and reducing the impact on native species in the hosting ecosystem.[5] Grasslands account for 30% of the world’s land area and have great potential to meet the demand for PV arrays, especially the deployment of PV arrays in grasslands, which will not preclude the ability of sheep to graze on the land around the PV arrays and provide shelter for sheep by the panels.[6][−][9] Therefore, grassland ecosystems rank highly in terms of their potential for PV array deployment.[10][−][12] In recent years, the installed PV capacity in Northeast China has increased rapidly.[13] For instance, the total planned developable capacity of PV projects in Jilin Province amounts to 36.14 GW

(by 2035), and dozens of concentrated solar power systems have been built in this province. The sustained flux global warming potential (SGWP) and the sustained flux global cooling potential (SGCP) are important indexes to measure a substance released into the atmosphere,[14] and they are also the key life cycle impact indicators to quantify the environmental performance of solar parks.[15] For PV modules manufactured in Europe and China, the life-cycle greenhouse gas (GHG) footprints were estimated to be 37.3 and 72.2 g CO2-eq kW h[−][1] , respectively.[16] Previous studies have considered the GHG footprint during the production, transportation, and waste treatment processes of solar parks.[17][−][19] However, such changes in land use may affect soil processes, plant community dynamics,[20] and GHG emissions in grassland ecosystems. Therefore, there is a lack of accurate measurements of GHG

emissions during the operation periods of solar parks, which may lead to an inaccurate assessment of the GHG footprint.

Reducing GHG emissions is one of the main advantages of PV power generation.[21] In simulation studies, research in Poland has calculated that a kilowatt of installed solar power saves up to NO2 by 16 kg, SO2 by 9 kg, and CO2 by 600−2300 kg compared to fossil fuels.[22] A 50 MW solar park could reduce CO2 emissions by up to 45 million tons compared with fossil fuels per year in Egypt.[23] Another report indicated that PV power generation was expected to reduce 46.5 Tg of CO2 emissions compared with 600 MW of coal-fired supercritical units in China.[24] In field studies, an experiment in a UK solar park through the net ecosystem carbon exchange result found that the reference zone outside the PV arrays and the gap zone between the adjacent panels tended to be a sink of CO2, but the sheltered zone under the PV panels was more often a source of CO2. However, no significant differences in soil properties were detected between treatments throughout the year.[10] Another experiment in southern France found that shading by PV panels significantly affected soil respiration. Specifically, compared with ambient blocks, a reduction in CO2 was detected in under panel blocks.[20] In summary, previous simulations and field studies have focused mostly on CO2 but less on N2O and CH4. Therefore, the study of GHG emissions during the operation period of solar parks is incomplete. Based on the technical characteristics of solar power, previous studies have stated that solar parks should have a long lifetime.[25] However, the GHG fluxes during the life cycle of solar parks in hosting ecosystems have not been quantified. When estimating the GHG footprint of PV power generation to supplement the defect of the impact of solar

parks on GHG emissions in hosting ecosystems, it is necessary to propose an evaluation model to quantify the influence of GHG emissions from the hosting ecosystem due to land use changes caused by solar parks.

The influence of the solar park on hosting ecosystems can be summarized as follows: first, solar park construction involves clearing and grading the soil surface, digging trenches to lay electric cables, which may contribute to part of vegetation loss, soil compaction, and increased erosion risks.[20] Second, solar park management may involve regular mowing and cleaning to avoid fire hazards and the loss of power generation caused by vegetation shading and dust accumulating on the PV panels.[26] Third, the operation period of solar parks in hosting ecosystems results in land use changes; large-scale PV arrays in solar parks have the potential to affect land surface albedo,[27] cause shading[28][,][29] and intercept precipitation.[30] Changes in surface albedo and soil moisture may directly and indirectly affect soil temperature.[31][−][33] The shading and intercept precipitation of PV panels may alter soil moisture patterns in grasslands.[34] Previous research found that shading by PV panels in desert locations might raise the soil temperature during the winter but reduce it during the other three seasons, and soil moisture in the shading zone was significantly higher than in ambient zones.[35] The sheltered zone was cool and dry in summer, but the gap zone between the PV panels was colder than the ambient zone and sheltered zone in winter; the PV arrays significantly affected the aboveground plant biomass and the plant species on the grassland.[10] PV panels could accelerate vegetation recovery by modifying the soil temperature and moisture conditions in an arid sandy ecosystem during the growing season.[36] A similar benefit for vegetation restoration

from PV arrays has been found in the Gobi Desert.[37] In short, PV arrays have the potential to alter the soil temperature and soil moisture during the operation period in grassland ecosystems. Previous studies in grassland ecosystems have demonstrated that soil temperature and soil moisture can influence GHG emissions by regulating soil organic matter mineralization, chemical reaction rates,[38][,][39] and gas diffusion in the soil,[40] stimulating the growth and activity of grass roots and microorganisms,[41] and altering microbial nitrification and denitrification processes.[42][,][43] Therefore, PV arrays are expected to have the potential to influence GHG emissions in grassland ecosystems. However, few studies have been conducted to investigate the driving factors of PV arrays that affect GHG emissions from their host grassland ecosystems.

This study investigated the air microclimate, vegetation characteristics, and soil properties of a solar park located in the Songnen Grassland, China, and measured the GHG fluxes (CO2, CH4, and N2O) and aimed to investigate the effect of PV arrays on the GHG fluxes due to differences in the soil properties and vegetation characteristics. We hypothesized that (1) the shelter of PV panels could cause a difference in air microclimate, vegetation characteristics, and soil properties between the PV arrays and ambient zones, with the difference in soil temperature and moisture affected by PV panels being the key factors driving the difference in GHG fluxes between the PV arrays and ambient zones and (2) PV arrays have continuous influence on hosting ecosystems’ GHG emissions throughout their life cycle, and ignoring such impacts would result in an overestimation of the GHG footprint of PV power generation.

## ■ **[MATERIALS][AND][METHODS]**

**Site Description.** This experiment was carried out at Honghua solar park (44°18′52′′N, 123°57′27′′E; 180 m a.s.l.), located in the Songnen Grassland, Northeast China (Figure 1) and constructed in 2018. This area has a typical temperate continental semi-arid climate with an average annual temperature of 6.4 °C. The average annual precipitation (1950− 2004) is 471 mm, with 80% of the precipitation occurring during the growing season (May to September). Prior to its conversion to a solar park, the vegetation of this field site was degraded saline meadow steppe. The plants are mainly _Leymus chinensis_ , accompanied by _Artemisia scoparia_ , _Chloris virgata_ , _Setaria viridis_ , _Lespedeza daurica_ , _Hordeum brevisubulatum_ , _Erigeron acris_ subsp., and _Saussurea runcinata_ . We compared these results with the environmental assessment data collected before the construction of the solar park and found that the plant composition did not change significantly after the solar park was built and operated for 3 years. According to the

Chinese vegetation classification and plant functional group division method,[44][,][45] the vegetation in the reference zone outside the PV arrays (Ambient), the gap zone between the PV panels (Gap), and the sheltered zone under the PV panels (Under)[10] was divided into three community types and named as the _L. chinensis_ community, the _A. scoparia_ community, and the Forb community according to the dominant species nomenclature. The solar park is protected by a fence, and the area around it (including Ambient, Gap, and Under) is completely closed to grazing. This area was regularly grazed before the solar park was installed. The soil types include meadow soils, saline-alkali soils, and chernozem.

The Honghua solar park occupies an area of approximately 100 ha and has an installed capacity of 40 MW. The PV panel module is a 275 W polycrystalline silicon PV panel with a size of 1640 mm × 990 mm × 35 mm. The PV panels are arranged on a slope vertically and fixed on columns. The length of the inclined plane of the solar panel module is 3320 mm. The entire solar park uses a total of 145,600 PV panels. The designed operation cycle of this solar park is 25 years, and the total power generation is 310492.13 MW h. The operation mode of the PV module is fixed bracket mode, and the azimuth angle is taken to be 0°, which means the module is facing ° south, and the tilt angle is 42 . The distance between two adjacent rows of PV panels is 12 meters.

Using three microclimate stations setup in the Ambient, Gap, and Under experimental zones, respectively. From 13/05/2021 12:00 to 30/09/21 12:00, the air microclimate parameters and photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) were measured every minute at one plot in each experimental zone, with the average for each hour recorded. At three experimental zones, air (150 cm above the surface) temperature, relative humidity (RH, 150 cm above the surface), and PAR (150 cm above the surface) were recorded (Horde, CN: HED Micro Station with T-HED-A001, H-HED-A001, and P-HED-M003). **Plant Sampling and Analysis.** A rectangular frame of 1 m[2] was placed on each plot. Plant height (Height) was recorded using a scale. The plant coverage (Cover) of all occurring plant species was estimated as the vertical projection of aboveground plant organs. A direct counting method was used to measure plant density (PD).

**Evaluation Model of the GHG Footprint during the Operation Period of PV Arrays.** We propose an evaluation model to quantify the incremental GHG emissions from hosting ecosystem during the life cycle of PV arrays. First, we calculated the areas of Under and Gap in the PV arrays and calculated the SGWP difference between Under and Ambient and between Gap and Ambient, respectively. Second, we multiplied the SGWP difference between the two zones and the Ambient by their areas to obtain the SGWP impact of the PV arrays in the hosting ecosystem and then multiplied the life cycle of the solar park. Finally, we divide the influence value of PV arrays in hosting ecosystem SGWP by the total power

output of the solar park, which is the GHG footprint of PV arrays in hosting ecosystem. The topography of the Honghua solar park is close to flat, and the ground slope is taken to be zero when performing calculations.

**Statistical Analyses.** All statistical analyses were conducted using R statistical software, version 4.1.3. Soil properties and vegetation characteristics between the treat-

ments were tested for significance by using a one-way ANOVA with the LSD multiple comparison (R package: rstatix 0.7.1). A repeated measures linear mixed model was used to examine the effects of different experimental zones (Zone), PCTs, and sampling months (Time) on GHG fluxes; Zone, PCT, and Time and their interactions were treated as fixed effects, and site was treated as a random effect (R package: lme4 1.1-31). We divided the _E_ h obtained in this study by the sum of the estimated carbon footprint of PV systems in previous studies and _E_ h, and used the result to represent the deviation value of the carbon footprint estimation of PV systems if _E_ h is not included in the carbon footprint estimation model of PV systems. In addition, we used structural equation models (SEMs; Grace, 2006) to examine direct and indirect mechanisms that regulate GHG fluxes using the lavaan SEM package in R. All SEM analyses were conducted independently for each GHG flux, and the conceptual model of hypothetical relationships based on theoretical knowledge was developed. Each model’s overall goodness-of-fit was tested using the chisquare test ( _c_[2] ; the good fit of the model when 0 ≤ _c_[2] ≤ 2 and 0 ≤ _p_ ≤ 1), the root mean square error of approximation (rmsea; the good fit of the model when 0 ≤ rmsea ≤ 0.05), the standardized root mean square residual (srmr; the good fit of the model when 0 ≤ srmr ≤ 0.05), and the comparative fit index (cfi; the good fit of the model when 0.97 ≤ cfi ≤ 1).[58][,][59]

## ■ **[RESULTS][AND][DISCUSSION]**

**Effect of the Solar Park on the Air Microclimates, Soil Properties, and Vegetation Characteristics.** This study revealed that PV arrays changed the air microclimates (Figure 2), soil properties (Figure 3), and vegetation characteristics (Table 1) during the operation period of the solar park hosting the grassland vegetation, which supports our first hypothesis. The results of soil temperature (Figure 3a) reduced by the PV panels’ shading were consistent with previous studies.[10][,][60] This reduction could be attributable to the interception of shortwave radiation by PV panels.[30] Our results and another field study in the grassland in Oxfordshire (UK)[10] showed that the soil moisture (Figure 3b) between the Ambient, the Gap, and the Under zones was not significantly different in the solar park hosting the grassland. The shading of PV panels leads to a lower VPD (Figure 2a) in the Under zones, resulting in a lower transpiration rate, which partially offsets the effect of the precipitation intercept on soil moisture caused by PV panels.[30] Besides, although PV panels can intercept and reallocate precipitation under the PV panels, the interception is not complete (Figure 1b). The gap at the splicing of PV panels may lead to part of the precipitation entering the Under.[37] Additionally, surface runoff that occurs during rainfall gradually spreads and infiltrates into the soil on a flat surface and tends to be evenly distributed within the soil.[61][−][63] Therefore, the differences in soil moisture among different experimental zones may be obscured. However, a previous study in Colorado (USA)[64] showed that the soil moisture in the Ambient zones was significantly lower than that in the Under zones in the solar park hosting the grassland. By comparison, we found that the soil moisture measurement in Colorado was sampled at a depth of 5 cm, while both this study and that in Oxfordshire were sampled at a depth of 10 cm. This difference in sampling depth may account for the difference in soil moisture, which means that the effect of PV panels on soil moisture in the Under zones may be more pronounced in shallower soils. We calculated that the GHG footprint of the Honghua solar park was 20.62 g CO2-eq kW h[−][1] (Figure 7b). Previous research estimated solar parks’ GHG footprint to be between 20.00 and 60.35 g CO2-eq kW h[−][1] .[16][,][75][−][85] According to this study, the GHG footprint of the PV arrays would increase by 25.46 to 50.76% (Figure 7c) if the hosting ecosystem were to be a grassland ecosystem. In the meantime, considering the diversity of PV arrays hosting ecosystems and the huge differences among different ecosystems, future studies should also pay attention to the impact of PV arrays on the GHG footprint of other hosting ecosystems. Furthermore, we suggest that the impact on the hosting ecosystem during different periods of PV array operation should be evaluated, as differences in vegetation and soil properties inside and outside the PV arrays may occur with changes in the microclimate caused by the PV arrays, which in turn leads to different influences on the ecosystem’s GHG footprint at different stages of the PV array’s life cycle.

**Key Factors Influencing the GHG Fluxes in PV Arrays.** The results of SEMs explained 55.9, 18.3, and 33.1% of the

total variation in CO2, CH4, and N2O fluxes, respectively (Figure 8). The SEM analysis showed that the influence of PV arrays on GHG fluxes in hosting grassland was mainly caused by the variation in soil temperature and soil moisture, supporting our third hypothesis. The significant positive correlation between soil temperature and CO2 and N2O fluxes (Figure 8a,c)[86][−][88] could be attributed to the fact that soil temperature affects the size of most soil microbial colonyforming units and facilitates the emission rates of CO2 and N2O.[89][,][90] The negative correlation between soil temperature and CH4 flux (Figure 8b) can be caused by the fact that an increase in soil temperature leads to a decrease in soil moisture, which limits the biological activity of methane-oxidizing bacteria.[91] On the other hand, soil moisture has a significant positive effect on N2O, which might be due to an increase in soil moisture promoting soil microorganisms to consume more nutrients involved in soil nitrification and denitrification processes, resulting in a rise in N2O.[92][−][94] Unlike the responses of the CH4 and N2O fluxes, the CO2 flux was not significantly affected by soil moisture, which was not thought to be a regulator of the carbon dioxide flux. Similar results have been reported in previous studies on grassland.[59][,][95] A possible reason for this result may be that soil temperature becomes an important determinant of CO2 flux when soil moisture is sufficient to support biological activity,[96][,][97] which is consistent with the results that the soil moisture was not a significant difference between the Ambient zones and PV arrays.

The main processes of PV arrays affecting grassland vegetation, such as shading by PV panels, changing the surface temperature and precipitation distribution, and affecting the evaporation of surface water are approximately the same in grasslands at different locations, as demonstrated by previous studies of solar parks in Oxfordshire (UK),[10] the South Moravian Region (CR),[98] and Southern France.[99] China’s grasslands cover 392.8 million ha, accounting for 40% of the national land area.[100][,][101] The _L. chinensis_ meadow selected for this study is located in the Songnen grassland in Northeastern China, which is the most typical and largest grassland type in China and has good representativeness. Therefore, we are confident that the field results of this study can be largely extended to grasslands in other parts of the world and are of general significance.
